metadata.title: The evolution of gender gaps in numeracy and literacy between childhood and young adulthood

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study combines nationally representative samples from TIMSS (1995), PIRLS (2001), PISA (2000), and PIAAC (2011/12) for a synthetic birth cohort (born 1984/85; PIRLS used as proxy at age 10). For school-based assessments (TIMSS/PIRLS/PISA), sampling is two-stage (schools then students/classes), while PIAAC is a household survey with complex stratified sampling. The authors state that survey weights are used throughout and that standard errors are computed using Jackknife or Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) depending on the study, with plausible values handled via the repest Stata package. No ML model training is reported; the analysis is regression/quantile regression-based, so the weighting/replication approach is used for inference rather than for predictive modeling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not report a specific missing-data handling strategy for the analytic samples (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation). Given that the study relies on IRT-scaled proficiency estimates and uses repest to handle plausible values and complex sampling, missingness treatment is likely embedded in the ILSA scaling procedures, but the authors do not document how missing background variables or incomplete responses were handled at the analysis stage. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling at the microdata level.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The main synthetic-cohort analysis uses a single birth cohort (born 1984/85) observed at different ages across TIMSS 1995 (age 9–10), PISA 2000 (age 15), and PIAAC 2011/12 (age 26–27). For literacy at age 10, PIRLS was not administered in 1995, so PIRLS 2001 is used as a proxy for the cohort’s literacy at age 10. The authors select only countries that participated in all four studies (11 countries for numeracy; 10 for literacy; 5 for both). For PIAAC, they select respondents born between 1983 and 1986 to obtain cohort-relevant sample sizes (~300 per country). They also exclude foreign-born individuals to increase representativeness of the synthetic cohort.

main_findings.target_variable: Gender gap in numeracy (male–female difference in standardized scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled gender gaps in numeracy (standardized SD units): age 9/10 = -0.029 (SE 0.012), age 15/16 = -0.087*** (SE 0.027), age 26/27 = -0.332*** (SE 0.067). Quantile/decile patterns: average gap at 10th percentile = 0.035 (age 15/16) and 0.123 (age 26/27); at 90th percentile = -0.081*** (age 15/16) and -0.337** (age 26/27). Robustness: moving-cohort pooled numeracy gaps (PISA cohorts to PIAAC): -0.144*** (age 20/21), -0.194*** (age 23/24), -0.209*** (age 26/27).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995, PISA 2000, and PIAAC 2011/12 data for a synthetic birth cohort, the study leveraged gender and (in extended PIAAC specifications) STEM-related career and numeracy skills use to analyze the gender gap in numeracy, finding that the male advantage grows from about 3% of a standard deviation at age 9/10 to about one-third of a standard deviation by age 26/27. This indicates that interventions to prevent early numeracy divergence—especially around the transition from compulsory to post-compulsory education—may be crucial because the gap widens substantially in young adulthood, and the study’s descriptive regression framework cannot establish causal effects.

main_findings.target_variable: Gender gap in literacy (female–male difference in standardized scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled gender gaps in literacy (standardized SD units): age 9/10 = 0.185*** (SE 0.025), age 15/16 = 0.307*** (SE 0.023), age 26/27 = -0.019 (SE 0.057). Table 3 pooled change: literacy gap increases by 12% of a standard deviation between age 9/10 and 15/16, then shrinks by 33% between age 15/16 and 26/27. Quantile patterns: average gap at 10th percentile = 0.467*** (age 15/16) and 0.123 (age 26/27); at 90th percentile = 0.166*** (age 15/16) and -0.073 (age 26/27). Extended PIAAC (age 26/27) controls: baseline = -0.013 (SE 0.041); controlling for STEM = 0.062 (SE 0.045) and remains not statistically significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2001, PISA 2000, and PIAAC 2011/12 data for a synthetic birth cohort, the study leveraged gender and (in extended PIAAC specifications) STEM-related career and reading/writing skills use to analyze the gender gap in literacy, finding that girls’ advantage peaks in adolescence (about 22–28% of a standard deviation) and then essentially disappears by age 26/27 (around -0.019 SD, not statistically significant). This indicates that literacy gaps may be more malleable than numeracy gaps after compulsory schooling, suggesting that policy should focus on sustaining reading/writing engagement through early adulthood while recognizing that the study’s descriptive, non-causal regression approach limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This paper studies how gender gaps evolve across the life course by combining cross-sectional large-scale assessments for a synthetic cohort (born 1984/85) observed at ages 9–10 (TIMSS 1995 for numeracy; PIRLS 2001 proxy for literacy), 15–16 (PISA 2000), and 26–27 (PIAAC 2011/12). The analysis uses survey weights and complex-design standard errors (Jackknife/BRR) and handles plausible values via repest, with scores standardized using the overall mean/SD across participating countries. The key results are descriptive: numeracy shows a growing male advantage (pooled gaps: -0.029 at age 9/10, -0.087 at 15/16, -0.332 at 26/27), while literacy shows an inverted-U pattern (0.185 at 9/10, 0.307 at 15/16, -0.019 at 26/27). Extended PIAAC regressions suggest that controlling for STEM-related careers halves the numeracy gap but does not make the literacy gap statistically significant. Limitations include the absence of ML prediction models, reliance on synthetic-cohort comparability across assessments, and no explicit microdata missing-data handling strategy reported.
